adaptiveTeachingHints.hint: Point-and-say relay: child touches each body part and says the word while the song plays.
Child says the Hindi body word first: 'Very good! Aapne kaha सिर. In English — head. Say head!'
Child says the Marathi body word first: 'खूप छान! डोकं. In English — head. Say head!'
Child names the wrong part: Miss Julie touches the same part on herself — 'Is THIS my nose?' Let the picture (body) decide, never say 'wrong'.
Any gesture counts: child points to the body part; Miss Julie supplies the word warmly and moves on.
'Our body knows the answer — touch it and it will tell you!' Body-pointing cannot be guessed wrong.
Child leads the song: calls the next body part for the class.
Two-part check: Miss Julie says the word, child points; then child says the word for a part Miss Julie points to.

recallDesign.activity: Child echoes 'head' right after Miss Julie while touching the head.
Miss Julie asks a fresh 'What is this?' for a part not just practised; child answers with no model.
Next session's warm-up: 'Show me and say — eyes!' Child produces the word unprompted; home task reports one body word in English.

review.notes: Syllabus facts verified against the official 2025 PDF. Pedagogy, Hindi/Marathi support lines and teaching moves are Talkora-original drafts awaiting a human teacher's review; synthetic example validation does not count as teacher approval.

prerequisiteSkills: No prior English assumed; KG 'My Body and Actions' (g00-l03) is helpful but optional.
Comfortable with whole-body imitation games.

grammarConcepts.childFriendlyFraming: 'My' means it belongs to me: my head, my hands. Everyone says 'my' about their own body.

speakingObjectives: Say 'This is my ___' while touching the named part.
Answer 'Where is your chin?' with 'This is / Here is my chin.'

teacherExplanationExamples.hi: अपना सिर छुओ — यह मेरा सिर है।
teacherExplanationExamples.mr: तुझं डोकं धर — हे माझं डोकं.

teacherExplanationExamples.en: What is this? This is my hand.
teacherExplanationExamples.hi: यह क्या है? यह मेरा हाथ है।

hindiExplanations: शरीर के अंगों के नाम पहले हिंदी में बच्चे जानते हैं — सिर, आँख, कान। अंग्रेज़ी शब्द वही चीज़ हैं: head, eyes, ears।
marathiExplanations: शरीराच्या अवयवांची नावं मराठीत माहीत आहेत — डोकं, डोळे, कान. इंग्रजी शब्द तेच आहेत: head, eyes, ears.
remediationStrategies: Body-part words are taught through touch first, speech second — a silent child still learns.
Keep the 'my' frame constant; change only the body word.
assessmentCriteria: Points correctly to at least 6 of 11 named body parts.
Says at least 4 body-part words with the 'This is my ___' frame.
masteryIndicators: INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING: answers 'What is this?' for a picture-shown part with no model in the same session.
DELAYED_RECALL: names at least 3 body parts in English at the start of the next session, unprompted.
revisionActivities: Reverse roles: Miss Julie touches a part, child names it.
Sing the song slowly with only 3 parts, then add one more each day.
entries.shortSpokenHomework: Touch and tell someone at home three body parts in English — head, eyes, nose are enough!

teachingStages.note: Miss Julie touches and names her own head/eyes/nose; children copy the gesture.
Sing 1.1 with actions; slow the tempo on each body word.

adaptiveTeachingHints.hint: Chain drill: each child asks the next 'What is your name?' — the book's own activity.
Child answers in Hindi ('मेरा नाम…'): 'Very good! Mera naam — in English: My name is… Try it!'
Child answers in Marathi ('माझं नाव…'): 'छान! माझं नाव — in English: My name is… Try it!'
Child answers 'Your name is…' (order lost): Miss Julie models with a puppet asking the puppet, child echoes the puppet's answer.
Miss Julie holds the flash card with the child's own name and answers FOR the child happily, inviting only a nod first.
'Only YOU know your name — nobody can guess this treasure!' Personal facts block guessing.
Child becomes the puppeteer: asks the whole class and picks who answers.
Two-step ladder: echo the full answer → finish the started frame ('My name is…') → answer alone.

recallDesign.activity: Child echoes 'My name is ___' once after the model.
Miss Julie turns to the child fresh: 'And YOU? What is your name?' Child answers without a model.
Next session's attendance game: child answers the roll with 'My name is ___' / 'I am fine, thank you.'

review.notes: Syllabus facts verified against the official 2025 PDF. Pedagogy, Hindi/Marathi support lines and teaching moves are Talkora-original drafts awaiting a human teacher's review; synthetic example validation does not count as teacher approval.

prerequisiteSkills: Can say their own name in the home language.
Has experienced turn-taking in a group.

grammarConcepts.concept: What is your name? — question frame
grammarConcepts.childFriendlyFraming: 'What' asks for information. The answer swaps 'your' for 'my': your name → MY name.

comprehensionGoals: Child recognises the difference between the question (What is your name?) and the answer (My name is ___).
speakingObjectives: Ask 'What is your name?' and answer with 'I am ___' / 'My name is ___'.
Say 'How are you?' — 'I am fine, thank you.'

teacherExplanationExamples.mr: तुझं नाव काय? — माझं नाव प्रिया.

teacherExplanationExamples.en: How are you? — I am fine, thank you.

teacherExplanationExamples.mr: तू कसा आहेस? — मी बरं, धन्यवाद.

hindiExplanations: सवाल में 'your' (तुम्हारा) आता है, जवाब में 'my' (मेरा)। 'What is your name?' — 'My name is…'
marathiExplanations: प्रश्नात 'your' (तुझं) येतं, उत्तरात 'my' (माझं). 'What is your name?' — 'My name is…'
remediationStrategies: Answer-first teaching: child produces their own name sentence before practising the question.
Capital-letter idea tied to each child's own name — personal, never abstract.
assessmentCriteria: Answers 'What is your name?' with a complete 'My name is ___' frame.
Uses 'I am fine, thank you.' in the How-are-you exchange.
masteryIndicators: INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING: child asks AND answers the name exchange with a peer, no teacher model.
DELAYED_RECALL: next-day roll-call answered in English without prompting.
revisionActivities: Puppet asks child; child answers; then swap.
Name-circle: every child says one classmate's name with 'Glad to meet you.'
entries.shortSpokenHomework: Ask one person at home 'What is your name?' in English and tell Miss Julie tomorrow what they said.

teachingStages.note: Miss Julie 'meets' a puppet: full exchange modelled.
Chain drill with flash cards, per the teacher note.
Children ask each other in pairs.
Frame swap your→my rehearsed with gesture (point away/point to self).

adaptiveTeachingHints.hint: Hidden-object game: child names the object Miss Julie partially reveals.
Child names it in Hindi: 'हाँ! मेज़. English mein — table. Say table!'
Child names it in Marathi: 'बरोबर! मेज. English madhye — table. Mhaṇ — table!'
Child says chair for table: line the two pictures side by side — 'Which one do we sit ON? Show me!' Pictures decide.
Child only points; Miss Julie names warmly: 'Yes — the clock!' and moves on.
'Look carefully — the picture will tell you.' Reveal the picture corner first; guessing needs no listening, looking does.
Child describes where the thing is: 'The clock is on the wall.'
Two-object choice ('fan or door?') before open naming.

recallDesign.activity: Child repeats 'table' right after Miss Julie while pointing.
Miss Julie asks 'Show me the…' for an object not just named; child points and names alone.
Home task: find one object from the list at home and tell its English name next session.

adaptiveTeachingHints.hint: Child performs AND calls the next instruction for the class.
Child acts first, words come in Hindi: 'शाबाश! बैठ गए. English — sit down. Say it!'
Child acts first: 'शाब्बास! बसली. English — sit down. Mhaṇ!'
Child turns left for 'Turn right': Miss Julie stands beside the child facing the same way — bodies decide, not 'wrong'.
Child does the action only — the body is the answer; words join when ready.
Actions cannot be faked: 'Let your feet do the listening!'
Child is the caller in Simon-says style rounds.
Do-then-say: action first, then the word; next round word first.

recallDesign.activity: Child echoes 'Hands up!' while doing it.
Child follows a fresh instruction not just practised, then names it.
Assembly drill next day (links to 1.5 assembly lines): child responds to 'Stand in a line' type English instructions.

prerequisiteSkills: Can imitate whole-body actions.
Has followed one-step instructions at home/school.

grammarConcepts.childFriendlyFraming: Instruction words are short bossy-words: Stand up! Sit down! Hands up! No name needed — the class all does it together.

speakingObjectives: Give one instruction to a peer (e.g. 'Hands up!').
Say what the action is called after performing it.

adaptiveTeachingHints.hint: Ability show-and-tell: each child demonstrates one 'I can ___' to the class.

Child recites the refrain alone when Miss Julie shows the rain card only.
Next rainy day (or next session): child says 'Tip-Tap!' when rain is mentioned — real-world recall.

adaptiveTeachingHints.hint: Child retells both animal wishes with picture cards, then adds their own wish for rain.
Child tells the story in Hindi: 'बहुत अच्छे! Now in English — the peacock says: Please rain!'
Child tells the story in Marathi: 'उत्तम! आता इंग्रजीत — the peacock says: Please rain!'
Child says 'the fish want rain': Miss Julie holds up ONE fish card — 'One fish says…' The picture count decides.
Child holds up the right animal card when Miss Julie reads each wish — participation without speech.
'Look at the picture — who is dancing? The picture tells you.'
Child plays the peacock/fish and performs the request lines with feeling.
Two-card choice (peacock or fish?) before open retelling.

recallDesign.activity: Child echoes 'Please rain!' with the cloud card raised.
Child answers fresh who-questions with the cards face-down, using one-word or frame answers.
Next session: child retells ONE wish unprompted from a single picture card.

grammarConcepts.childFriendlyFraming: 'Please' is the polite-magic word for asking. Please rain! Please give me water. We use it when we want something.

comprehensionGoals: Answers who/what questions about the story.
Sequences: dark cloud → peacock's wish → fish's wish.
speakingObjectives: Says one story line with a picture prompt: 'The peacock says: Please rain!'
Makes one polite request with 'Please ___.

teacherExplanationExamples.en: The peacock says: 'Please rain, I want to dance!'
teacherExplanationExamples.hi: मोर कहता है: 'कृपया बारिश, मैं नाचना चाहता/चाहती हूँ!'
teacherExplanationExamples.mr: मोर म्हणतो: 'कृपया पाऊस, मला नाचायचं आहे!'

hindiExplanations: कहानी सुनो, तस्वीर बताएगी — बादल, मोर, मछली। फिर अंग्रेज़ी में एक इच्छा बोलो: 'Please rain!'
marathiExplanations: गोष्ट ऐका, चित्र सांगेल — ढग, मोर, मासे. मग इंग्रजीत एक इच्छा म्हणा: 'Please rain!'
remediationStrategies: Story-first, language-second: enjoyment carries the words.
Echoing (mist-032) is caught by the face-down-card check — repetition alone is never accepted as understanding.
assessmentCriteria: Answers 2/3 story who/what questions correctly.
Produces one 'Please ___' request.
masteryIndicators: INDEPENDENT_ANSWERING: answers story questions with cards face-down (cannot echo).
DELAYED_RECALL: retells one wish next session from a single prompt card.
revisionActivities: Polite-request role plays (Please give me the chalk.).
entries.shortSpokenHomework: Tell someone at home what the peacock and the fish asked the rain for — in English or mixed.
